title: Async all the way
sub: How to really cure a deadlock
cards/0/body:
If the inside is asynchronous, the outside should await too, all the way up to the event handler or Main. That's async all the way. Waiting for a task synchronously (.Result, .Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()) is called sync-over-async: in a UI it gives you a deadlock, on a server it gives you thread-pool starvation.

Why await cures the deadlock (the "after" code below):

  • 1. The await in the handler sees an unfinished task and returns control, so the UI thread is free and keeps running its queue.
  • 2. The response arrives, GetDataAsync's continuation comes via Post into the queue, and the UI thread runs it.
  • 3. The GetDataAsync task completes, the handler's continuation joins the queue, and label.Text changes on the UI thread.

No thread is blocked, so there's no waiting loop.
cards/0/deep: If the caller can't be async (a constructor, Dispose, a synchronous interface): a static async Task<T> CreateAsync() factory, IAsyncDisposable, an async version of the interface. If there's truly no way around blocking: GetAwaiter().GetResult() with ConfigureAwait(false) along the whole chain, and only off the UI thread.
cards/1/task: Fix the deadlock properly: no ConfigureAwait, just make the handler async.
cards/2/q: Why is await better than .Result in a WPF handler?
cards/2/options/0: The UI thread isn't blocked: continuations and clicks run, and no waiting loop forms
cards/2/options/1: The code is shorter, the behavior is the same
cards/2/options/2: With await the network answers faster
cards/2/explain: No blocked thread, no waiting loop.
cards/3/body: Since C# 7.1, Main can be async Task Main(). Event handlers are async void: the one sensible place for void. ASP.NET Core controllers return Task<IActionResult>.
cards/3/deep: async Task Main is a generated Main that calls Main().GetAwaiter().GetResult(). The console's main thread really does block, and that's fine: there's no context, so the pool runs the continuations.
cards/4/explain: .Result holds a pool thread for the entire database query.
cards/5/explain: async in the declaration, await before the call.
cards/6/body:
Wrapping a blocking synchronous call or a long computation in Task.Run and calling the method …Async is a lie. A thread is still busy, just a different one: a pool thread. On a server that's an extra switch and a pool thread tied up under the guise of asynchrony.

A truly asynchronous method waits without a thread (I/O through the OS). If there's no such API, the library exposes an honest synchronous method, and the caller decides whether Task.Run is needed: yes in a UI, to keep the window from freezing; no on a server.
cards/6/deep: Files are subtler: on Linux, .NET performs asynchronous reads of regular files on pool threads, because the OS has no convenient async API for them. But that's the platform's doing, not your library's; for sockets and networking, thread-free waiting exists everywhere.
cards/7/q: In a library: public Task<byte[]> HashAsync(byte[] d) => Task.Run(() => SHA256.HashData(d)); What's wrong?
cards/7/options/0: The method ties up a pool thread while posing as asynchronous; whether to use Task.Run is the caller's call
cards/7/options/1: Nothing: Task.Run makes the method truly asynchronous
cards/7/options/2: Task.Run can't be called inside a library; it's a compile error
cards/7/explain: The computation still occupies a thread, just a pool thread. In a UI the caller will wrap the synchronous HashData in Task.Run itself, and on a server it doesn't need the extra switch.
cards/8/q: Which of these are sync-over-async? Select all that apply.
cards/8/explain: Any synchronous wait on a task blocks the thread. GetAwaiter().GetResult() only throws the exception without the AggregateException wrapper; it blocks just the same.
